Historical Examples of Statistical Plots

A Course on Data Visualization

Livio Finos, University of Padova

2026-09-22

Overview

This document presents four foundational examples in the history of data visualization, featuring pioneering work by William Playfair, Florence Nightingale, John Snow, and Charles Minard. These visualizations established core principles still used in modern statistical graphics.

William Playfair (1759–1823): Bar Charts and Line Charts

Playfair is widely regarded as the inventor of modern statistical graphics. His 1786 Commercial and Political Atlas introduced both the line chart and the first known bar chart. 123

Line Chart Example

  1. A time-series plot showing England’s exports and imports to and from Denmark & Norway from 1700 to 1780. The area between the two lines is shaded to show the balance of trade (“Balance in Favour of England” vs. “Balance Again

Key features: - Two time series plotted on the same axes - Shaded area between lines to visualize trade balance - X-axis: years (1700–1780) - Y-axis: monetary value (imports/exports)

Bar Chart Example

  1. A horizontal bar chart showing Scotland’s exports (solid black bars) and imports (ribbed bars) to and from 17 different trading partners for the year Christmas 1780 to Christmas 1781. This is considered the first quantitative graphical form that did not locate data in space or time. 456

Key features: - Horizontal bars for categorical comparison - Paired bars for exports vs. imports - 17 trading partners on the y-axis - Monetary values on the x-axis

Florence Nightingale (1820–1910): Polar Area Diagrams

Nightingale developed the polar area diagram (also called the “coxcomb” or “Nightingale rose diagram”) to communicate mortality data from the Crimean War (1853–56). 789

Structure

  • A circle divided into 12 equal-angle wedges (one per month)
  • The area of each wedge (not just the radius) is proportional to the mortality rate
  • Each wedge is color-coded:
    • Blue: deaths from preventable diseases
    • Red: deaths from wounds
    • Black: deaths from other causes

Purpose

To show that most deaths were from preventable diseases and that mortality dropped dramatically after sanitary reforms were implemented in March 1855. 1011

Resources

  • Lehigh Library Exhibits: Nightingale’s Rose Diagram
  • Wikimedia Commons: Nightingale Rose Chart
  • Protovis: Nightingale’s Rose
  • University of St Andrews: Florence Nightingale PDF

John Snow (1813–1858): Cholera Maps

Snow’s 1854 map of the Broad Street cholera outbreak in London’s Soho district is a foundational example of spatial epidemiology and data visualization. 121314

Design

  • A street map showing individual cholera deaths as stacked black bars (or rectangles) at each address
  • Locations of public water pumps marked as circles
  • Focus on the Broad Street pump area

Insight

The clustering of deaths around the Broad Street pump provided visual evidence that cholera was waterborne, not airborne (as the miasma theory claimed). This work helped establish the germ theory of disease. 1516

Resources

  • Wikimedia Commons: Snow Cholera Map
  • Flourish: Recreating John Snow’s Cholera Map
  • ArcGIS: Map a Historic Cholera Outbreak
  • Lehigh Library Exhibits: Dr. John Snow’s Cholera Map
  • The John Snow Archive and Research Companion

Charles Minard (1781–1870): Napoleon Campaign Visualization

Minard’s 1869 Carte figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l’Armee Française dans la campagne de Russie 1812–1813 is often called “the best statistical graphic ever drawn” by Edward Tufte. 171819

Six Variables in Two Dimensions

Variable Encoding
Army size Width of the band (1 mm = 10,000 men), starting at 422,000 and ending at 10,000
Geography Latitude and longitude (the graphic is a map)
Direction of travel Color (tan/gold for advance, black for retreat)
Temperature Line graph at the bottom shows plummeting temperatures during the retreat
Time Dates along the retreat path
Location Relative to key cities, geographic markers, and battle sites
